text:
3.1 The Data
Two data sets are used to create the choropleth maps:

Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea), downloadable at data.gov.sg. This is geospatial data consisting of the geographical boundary of Singapore at planning subzone level, based on the URA Master Plan 2019. I have it as GeoJSON rather than the KML the reference material uses.
Singapore Residents by Planning Area / Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2024 in csv format (respopagesextod2024.csv), downloadable from the Department of Statistics, Singapore. This is aspatial data. It contains no coordinate values, but its PA and SZ fields serve as unique identifiers to georeference against the Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary.

Hands-on_Ex01/
└── data/
    ├── geospatial/
    │   └── MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaGEOJSON.geojson
    └── aspatial/
        └── respopagesextod2024.csv






ImportantCorrection to the reference material



Note the change of boundary vintage from Hands-on Exercise 1A. That exercise used the Master Plan 2014 boundary. This one uses the Master Plan 2019 boundary.

  st_transform(crs = 3414)

3.2.1 Checking the attribute columns
First I check what columns came through, so I know whether any tidying is needed.

[11] "FMEL_UPD_D" "SHAPE.AREA" "SHAPE.LEN"  "geometry"  








ImportantWhy the reference material’s whole “tidying” step is skipped here



The reference chapter’s KML stores its attributes inside an HTML table buried in a single Description field, so it has to write a helper function with rvest to scrape REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N, SUBZONE_N and SUBZONE_C back out as columns:
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}
The GeoJSON does not need any of that. As the names(mpsz) output shows, it already carries SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, REGION_N and SUBZONE_C as ordinary columns, so there is nothing to scrape. I keep rvest loaded in Section 2 only for completeness against the reference material; it is not actually exercised in my version.
The one small schema difference worth noting: my file names its area and length fields SHAPE.AREA and SHAPE.LEN (the reference material’s shapefile used SHAPE_Leng / SHAPE_Area). I don’t use either in this exercise, so it has no effect on the analysis.

3.3 Importing Attribute Data into R
read_csv() of readr imports respopagesextod2024.csv into a tibble called popdata.

popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
3.4 Data Preparation
Before a thematic map can be prepared, I need a data table containing the variables PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, and DEPENDENCY:

YOUNG: age group 0 to 4 through age group 20 to 24,
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age group 25 to 29 through age group 60 to 64,
AGED: age group 65 and above,
TOTAL: all age groups, and
DEPENDENCY: the ratio of young plus aged against the economy active group.







ImportantCorrection to the reference material



The reference chapter instructs the reader to “prepare a data table with year 2020 values,” but the file it imports is respopagesextod2024.csv and every object it creates is named popdata2024. The reference to 2020 is a leftover from an earlier edition. The data being prepared is June 2024.



3.4.1 Data wrangling
The functions used are pivot_wider() of tidyr, and mutate(), filter(), group_by() and select() of dplyr.






ImportantThe most serious correction in this exercise



The reference chapter builds YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE and AGED using positional column indexing on the pivoted table:
mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6]) + rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11]) + rowSums(.[13:15])) %>%
mutate(`AGED` = rowSums(.[16:21]))
Those hard-coded positions are only correct if pivot_wider() lays the age-group columns out in one specific order. It does not for my file, and the result is silently wrong.
The problem is that pivot_wider() orders the new columns by the alphabetical sort of the AG values, not their numerical age order. When I actually inspect the pivoted column order (next chunk), 5_to_9 lands at column 14, sorted after 45_to_49 and 50_to_54, because “5” sorts after “4”. That single displacement throws off the reference formula in two places:

YOUNG is meant to be ages 0 to 24. The formula .[3:6] + .[12] captures 0_to_4, 10_to_14, 15_to_19, 20_to_24 and then, via column 12, 50_to_54. It misses 5_to_9 entirely and wrongly folds in 50-to-54-year-olds.
ECONOMY ACTIVE is meant to be ages 25 to 64. Its ranges pull in column 14, which is 5_to_9, so primary-school-age children get counted as working adults.

Only AGED (cols 16 to 21) happens to land correctly. The upshot is that the dependency ratio, the single variable this whole exercise maps, comes out wrong for every subzone.
I fix this by selecting age groups by name rather than by position, so it is correct regardless of how pivot_wider() happens to order the columns.


First, to make the problem visible, here is the actual column order pivot_wider() produces:

popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(POP = sum(Pop), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG, values_from = POP) %>%
  names()

 [1] "PA"          "SZ"          "0_to_4"      "10_to_14"    "15_to_19"   
 [6] "20_to_24"    "25_to_29"    "30_to_34"    "35_to_39"    "40_to_44"   
[11] "45_to_49"    "50_to_54"    "55_to_59"    "5_to_9"      "60_to_64"   
[16] "65_to_69"    "70_to_74"    "75_to_79"    "80_to_84"    "85_to_89"   
[21] "90_and_over"


Note where 5_to_9 sits in that list. It is not adjacent to 0_to_4.
Now the corrected, name-based wrangling:

young_ages <- c("0_to_4", "5_to_9", "10_to_14", "15_to_19", "20_to_24")

econ_ages <- c("25_to_29", "30_to_34", "35_to_39", "40_to_44",
               "45_to_49", "50_to_54", "55_to_59", "60_to_64")

aged_ages <- c("65_to_69", "70_to_74", "75_to_79", "80_to_84",
               "85_to_89", "90_and_over")

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(POP = sum(Pop), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG, values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(
    YOUNG            = rowSums(across(all_of(young_ages))),
    `ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(across(all_of(econ_ages))),
    AGED             = rowSums(across(all_of(aged_ages)))
  ) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = YOUNG + `ECONOMY ACTIVE` + AGED) %>%
  mutate(DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(PA, SZ, YOUNG, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY)







Note



Two smaller points on top of the main fix:

across(all_of(...)) is the current tidyverse for summing a named set of columns. If any named column is missing, it would fail which is exactly the behaviour I want.
The reference chapter’s summarise() omits the .groups argument, which prints a grouping message and leaves the tibble grouped, so it then calls ungroup() on the next line. Passing .groups = "drop" does the same thing in one step and suppresses the message.





3.4.2 Joining the attribute data and geospatial data
Before the georelational join, the values in PA and SZ must be converted to uppercase, because those fields contain a mix of upper and lowercase while SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N are entirely uppercase.

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ), 
            .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

Next, left_join() of dplyr joins the geographical data and attribute table using planning subzone name (SUBZONE_N and SZ) as the common identifier.

mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

left_join() is used with the mpsz simple feature data frame as the left table specifically so that the output stays a simple features data frame. Reversing the order would return a plain tibble and every subsequent tm_shape() call would fail.
Before going on I check how well the join actually matched, since a name-based join across two independently maintained data sets rarely matches perfectly:

sum(is.na(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY))

[1] 94








ImportantAn unexplained gap in the reference material



The reference chapter’s own summary() output later reports NA values in DEPENDENCY but never explains where they come from or what to do about them.
They arise from two distinct causes worth separating: subzones that genuinely have no resident population (industrial estates, water catchment areas, port land, military zones), and subzones whose names differ between the URA boundary file and the SingStat population file so the join simply fails to match.
This matters for map interpretation. tmap shades missing values in grey by default, and a reader looking at a grey subzone cannot tell whether it means “nobody lives here” or “the join broke.” I identify which subzones are affected in the Extras.



write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")

text:
4.1 Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using qtm()
The quickest way to draw a choropleth map with tmap is qtm(). It is concise and provides good default visualisation in many cases.

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(mpsz_pop2024, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")








tmap_mode() with the "plot" option produces a static map. "view" produces an interactive one. The fill argument maps the attribute to be shaded.

section: 4.2 Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
text:
4.2 Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
The disadvantage of qtm() is that it makes the aesthetics of individual layers harder to control. For a high quality cartographic choropleth map, tmap’s drawing elements should be used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(col_alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))














ImportantCorrection to the reference material



The reference chapter writes this as tm_grid(alpha = 0.2). In tmap version 4 the bare alpha argument was split into role-specific forms, col_alpha for line or border colour transparency and fill_alpha for fill transparency. Passing alpha to tm_grid() under version 4 will either warn or be silently ignored depending on the point release. I used col_alpha, which is the version 4 equivalent for grid lines.
The same chapter also spells the URA as “Urban Redevelopment Authorithy” in the credits string. Corrected above.



4.2.1 Drawing a base map
The basic building block of tmap is tm_shape() followed by one or more layer elements such as tm_polygons(), tm_symbols(), tm_lines(), tm_raster() and tm_text().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()








By default, polygon areas are plotted in light grey (gray85) and polygon borders in a slightly darker grey (gray25).


4.2.2 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_polygons()
To shade by a selected variable, that variable is assigned to tm_polygons().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")








Things to note about tm_polygons():

The default interval binning is called “pretty”.
The default colour scheme is blues3 of ColorBrewer.
Missing values are shaded in grey by default.



4.2.3 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_fill() and tm_borders()
tm_polygons() is a wrapper of tm_fill() and tm_borders(). tm_fill() shades the polygons using the default colour scheme. tm_borders() adds the borders of the polygon features.
Using tm_fill() alone:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








The subzones are shaded according to their dependency values, but with no boundaries drawn. Adding tm_borders():

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()








Light-grey border lines have now been added. The fill_alpha argument defines transparency between 0 (fully transparent) and 1 (opaque). Besides fill_alpha, tm_borders() takes three other arguments:

col for border colour,
lwd for border line width, default 1, and
lty for border line type, default "solid".


tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60", 
             lwd = 0.1, 
             lty = "dashed")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
4.3 Data classification methods of tmap
Most choropleth maps employ some method of data classification. The point of classification is to take a large number of observations and group them into data ranges or classes. tmap provides ten data classification methods: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks.






NoteFrom the lesson slides



The choice of classification method is not cosmetic. It changes which spatial pattern the reader sees.

Quantile puts the same number of features in each class. Good for showing rank, but can group very different values together.
Equal interval divides the value range into equally sized classes. The slides caution against this when data is skewed or has large outliers, because outliers produce empty classes.
Jenks (natural breaks) finds natural groupings by statistical optimisation.
Standard deviation is appropriate when the distribution approximates normal.

The slides also note there is no ideal number of classes. More classes means less generalisation but worse legibility, and 4 to 7 is the usual working range.



4.3.1 Plotting choropleth maps with built-in classification methods
Quantile classification with 5 classes:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Equal interval classification:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








The quantile classification is far more evenly distributed than the equal interval one. The reason is visible in the summary statistics further below: DEPENDENCY has a much larger maximum than its median, so equal interval spends almost all of its classes on an empty upper range and crushes nearly every subzone into the bottom class. This is exactly the skew case the lesson slides warn about.


4.3.2 Plotting a choropleth map with custom breaks
For all built-in styles, the category breaks are computed internally. To override these defaults, breakpoints can be set explicitly with the breaks argument of tm_scale_intervals(). In tmap, breaks include a minimum and maximum, so to end up with n categories, n+1 elements must be specified in increasing order.
It is good practice to get descriptive statistics on the variable before setting break points.

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
 0.0000  0.6750  0.7283  0.7563  0.8140 10.0000      94 








ImportantCorrection to the reference material



The reference chapter says: “we set break point at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90. In addition, we also need to include a minimum and maximum, which we set at 0 and 100. Our breaks vector is thus c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00).”
There are two problems here.
First, the text contradicts itself. It says the maximum is set at 100, then gives a vector ending at 1.00.
Second, and more seriously, 1.00 is almost certainly the wrong maximum. The summary output shows DEPENDENCY reaching well above 1.00. Any subzone with a dependency ratio above 1.00 falls outside the break range entirely and is rendered as a missing value, shaded grey, indistinguishable from the subzones that are genuinely NA.
So the reference map silently hides real data and mislabels it as missing. The fix is to close the upper break at or above the observed maximum. I use 100 below, which matches the chapter’s stated intent and comfortably covers the real maximum.



tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 100))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








To make the consequence explicit, here are the two versions side by side. The map on the left uses the reference chapter’s break vector, the one on the right uses the corrected version.

map_broken <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Upper break at 1.00 (values above are dropped)")

map_fixed <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 100))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Upper break at 100 (all values retained)")

tmap_arrange(map_broken, map_fixed, asp = 1, ncol = 2)








Counting exactly how many subzones the reference version loses:

sum(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY > 1.00, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 3

text:
4.4 Colour Scheme
tmap supports colour ramps either defined by the user or drawn from the predefined ramps of the RColorBrewer package.

4.4.1 Using a ColorBrewer palette
The preferred palette is assigned to the values argument of tm_scale_intervals().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








To reverse the colour shading, a - prefix is added:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)














Note



The reference chapter describes this as assigning “the preferred colour to palette argument of values,” which conflates two things. In tmap version 3 the argument was palette. In version 4 it is values. There is no palette argument inside tm_scale_intervals() any more, only values.




4.4.2 Cartographic furniture
Besides map style, tmap provides arguments to draw map furniture such as a compass, scale bar, and grid lines.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, col_alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
4.5 Map Layout
Map layout refers to the combination of all map elements into a cohesive whole: background, frame, typography, scale, aspect ratio, margins, and more.

4.5.1 Map legend
tmap provides several legend options to change placement, format and appearance.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio",
                position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, col_alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))














ImportantCorrection to the reference material



The reference chapter adds tm_pos_auto_in() as a standalone map element in the chain:
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(...) +
  tm_pos_auto_in() +          # <- this line
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  ...
This is a misuse of the function. tm_pos_auto_in() is a position specifier, not a map layer. It is meant to be passed to the position argument of a component such as tm_legend(), not added to the map with +. Used as written, it either errors or is silently discarded, and the legend position never changes, which defeats the point of a section titled “Map Legend”.
I moved the positioning into tm_legend(position = ...) above, where it actually takes effect.




4.5.2 Map style
tmap allows a wide variety of layout settings to be changed globally via tmap_style().

tmap_style("natural")

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Resetting to the default style:

tmap_style("white")







ImportantCorrection to the reference material



The reference chapter appends tmap_style("natural") to the end of the map chain with a +:
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(...) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")        # <- this line
tmap_style() is not a tmap element. It is a global options setter that returns the previous style invisibly. It cannot be added to a map object with +. Written this way it either errors, or worse, sets the style as a side effect after the map has already been composed, so the style applies to the next map rather than this one.
The correct usage is to call it as a standalone statement before the map, as I did above, and to reset it afterwards so it does not silently leak into every subsequent chunk in the document. The same error appears again in the reference chapter’s small-multiples section.

ImportantCorrection to the reference material



Two issues in the reference chapter’s version of this chunk.
First, it passes ncols = 3 to tm_facets(). The argument is ncol, singular, consistent with nrow immediately above it and with tmap_arrange(). ncols is not a recognised argument and the intended 2 by 3 grid never materialises.
Second, it passes title arguments to tm_layout():

          title.position = c("center", "center"),
          title.size = 20)
In tmap version 4, title handling moved out of tm_layout() into the dedicated tm_title() component. These title.* arguments are version 3 holdovers. There is also no title text supplied anywhere in the chunk, so title.position and title.size are positioning something that does not exist. I dropped them rather than reproduce a no-op.

9.2 Comparing all classification methods side by side
The lesson slides stress that classification method choice changes what the reader sees. Rather than take that on faith, I plot four methods on identical data and compare.

make_map <- function(style_name, label) {
  tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                  style = style_name,
                  n = 5,
                  values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(
                  position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
                  text.size = 0.5)) +
    tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.4) +
    tm_title(label, size = 0.9)
}

tmap_arrange(
  make_map("quantile", "Quantile"),
  make_map("equal",    "Equal interval"),
  make_map("jenks",    "Jenks / natural breaks"),
  make_map("sd",       "Standard deviation"),
  ncol = 2, nrow = 2
)








The four maps use the same variable, the same palette, and the same number of classes, yet they tell noticeably different stories. Equal interval and standard deviation are both dominated by the outlier subzones and flatten almost everything else into one class.

9.4 Unclassed (continuous) choropleth
The lesson slides distinguish classed from unclassed choropleth maps. tmap supports the latter through tm_scale_continuous(), which drops binning entirely and maps values onto a continuous colour ramp.

ClassedUnclassed



tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.pu_bu_gn"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency")) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_title("Classed: 5 quantile classes")











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(
                limits = c(0, 2),
                outliers.trunc = c(TRUE, TRUE),
                values = "brewer.pu_bu_gn"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency")) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_title("Unclassed: continuous ramp, truncated at 2.0")











The unclassed version preserves every value distinction but is harder to read off precisely, since a reader cannot tell a 0.83 from a 0.87. The classed version generalises but is legible. Which is preferable depends on whether the map is for exploration or for communication.

text:
6.2 Clark-Evans test with Monte Carlo simulation
Here method = "MonteCarlo" is used, so the p-value is computed by comparing the observed R value against nsim simulated realisations of Complete Spatial Randomness.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                clipregion = sg_owin,
                alternative = c("clustered"),
                method = "MonteCarlo",
                nsim = 99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








NoteQuiz




What statistical conclusion can I draw from this Monte Carlo version of the test?
How does this result compare with the asymptotic test in 6.1?

My answer: Same R value, p = 0.01, so I still reject the null hypothesis and reach the same clustering conclusion as 6.1. The two p-values look very different, but that is because the Monte Carlo p-value is bounded below by roughly 1/(nsim+1), so with nsim = 99 it cannot go smaller than 0.01. Both tests agree on the direction and significance of the result.

11.1 Quadrat analysis as a cross-check on Clark-Evans
The lecture slides cover quadrat analysis and the Variance-Mean Ratio (VMR) as a way to test Complete Spatial Randomness, but the reference material did not show this. I found it worth trying quadrat.test() on the same childcareSG_ppp object I already tested with Clark-Evans, so I can compare the two conclusions side by side.

qt <- quadrat.test(childcareSG_ppp, nx = 5, ny = 5)
qt


    Chi-squared test of CSR using quadrat counts

data:  childcareSG_ppp
X2 = 713, df = 21, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Quadrats: 22 tiles (irregular windows)



plot(unmark(childcareSG_ppp), main = "Quadrat counts for childcare centres")
plot(qt, add = TRUE, cex = 0.7, col = "red")














TipWhy I wanted to explore this



Clark-Evans and quadrat analysis test the same null hypothesis of Complete Spatial Randomness, but from different angles. Clark-Evans is distance-based and looks at nearest neighbour spacing, while quadrat analysis is count-based and looks at how evenly points are spread across a grid of cells. I found that when both tests agree, that gives me more confidence in the conclusion. When they disagree, it usually means the pattern is scale-dependent, for example clustered at a fine scale but more even at a coarse scale, which a single test on its own would not reveal.

11.2 A more robust density comparison across planning areas
Section 10.3 plots four KDE surfaces side by side, but each one uses its own bw.diggle() bandwidth, so the colour scales are not directly comparable panel to panel. I found it more defensible to compute a single shared bandwidth across the combined point pattern first, then reuse that same sigma value for all four areas.

# combine all four ppp objects to get one shared bandwidth
childcare_all_ppp.km <- superimpose(childcare_pg_ppp.km,
                                     childcare_tm_ppp.km,
                                     childcare_ck_ppp.km,
                                     childcare_jw_ppp.km)
shared_bw <- bw.diggle(childcare_all_ppp.km)
shared_bw

    sigma 
0.4851187 



par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(density(childcare_pg_ppp.km, sigma = shared_bw, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
     main = "Punggol")
plot(density(childcare_tm_ppp.km, sigma = shared_bw, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
     main = "Tampines")
plot(density(childcare_ck_ppp.km, sigma = shared_bw, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
     main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(density(childcare_jw_ppp.km, sigma = shared_bw, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
     main = "Jurong West")














TipWhy I wanted to explore this



This step shows me that comparing density surfaces fairly across regions requires a shared bandwidth, not one independently optimised per region. Using per-area bandwidths, as in section 10.3, is a fragile pattern that can make two areas with genuinely similar density look visually different just because the bandwidth selector picked different sigma values. It is a small change but it changes what conclusions I am allowed to draw from the comparison.

            LENGTHUNIT["metre",1]]],
    PRIMEM["Greenwich",0,

    CS[ellipsoidal,2],
        AXIS["geodetic latitude (Lat)",north,
            ORDER[1],
            ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
        AXIS["geodetic longitude (Lon)",east,
            ORDER[2],
            ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
    ID["EPSG",4326]]


This correctly reports EPSG:4326 (WGS84).






NoteWhy the reference material’s EPSG-9001 problem doesn’t appear here



The reference chapter spends a subsection fixing a wrongly labelled CRS. Its shapefile’s .prj file is incomplete, so st_crs() reports EPSG 9001, which isn’t even a coordinate system (it’s the EPSG code for the unit metre), instead of the correct 3414. The fix there is st_set_crs(), which relabels metadata without moving any coordinates.
That specific failure mode is a shapefile artefact. .prj files are a separate sidecar file that’s easy to omit or corrupt during a shapefile export. GeoJSON has no equivalent sidecar to go missing. The CRS is either implied as WGS84 by the format spec (as here) or stated explicitly inside the file itself. So there is no mislabelled CRS bug to fix in this data, and st_set_crs() isn’t the right tool here since my CRS label is already correct. What I need instead is a genuine coordinate transformation, covered next.

9.1 Use case 1: Land acquisition analysis

9.1.1 The scenario
The authority is planning to upgrade the existing cycling path. To do so, they need to acquire 5 metres of reserved land on both sides of the existing cycling path. I am tasked to determine the extent of the land needing to be acquired and its total area.


9.1.2 The solution

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath3414, 
                            dist = 5, 
                            nQuadSegs = 30)







Note



dist = 5 is interpreted in the units of the layer’s CRS. Because cyclingpath3414 has already been transformed to svy21 (metres), this correctly produces a 5 metre buffer. Had I skipped Section 7.2 and buffered the original wgs84 cyclingpath instead, dist = 5 would have been read as 5 degrees, roughly 550 km. That is exactly why the transform in Section 7 matters regardless of the overlay in Section 6 having looked fine.



buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))

  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
4.1 Reading the national file

kelurahan <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                     layer = "Batas_Wilayah_KelurahanDesa_10K_AR")

That gave me 83,518 features for the whole country, geometry type MULTIPOLYGON, sitting in WGS84. The .prj says GCS_WGS_1984, so EPSG:4326. I am glad I checked the CRS early, because the fire coordinates are also plain lon/lat degrees. Both files start life in the same reference system, so nothing is misaligned before I project.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
section: 4.2 Finding the right field before I filter anything
text:
4.2 Finding the right field before I filter anything
I really did not want to filter on a province name and get it slightly wrong. The attribute table is a thicket of code fields (KDPBPS, WADMKC, WADMKD, and so on). The province name turns out to live in WADMPR. Rather than take that on faith, I pulled the exact spelling straight from the data.

sort(unique(kelurahan$WADMPR))
grep("Bangka", kelurahan$WADMPR, value = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE) |> unique()

The grep gives back exactly one value, "Kepulauan Bangka Belitung", with no trailing spaces and no second spelling hiding in the list. Good. That is the string to filter on, and now I know it is the only one.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
4.3 Filtering to the province

babel <- kelurahan[kelurahan$WADMPR == "Kepulauan Bangka Belitung", ]
nrow(babel)

nrow(babel) comes back as 394. A sensible next check is whether any sub-district got recorded twice, since duplicate rows would inflate that count.

sum(duplicated(babel$OBJECTID))

Every OBJECTID is unique, so nothing is duplicated.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
4.4 Dropping the Z dimension
My first attempt to write babel out failed. GDAL threw an error about a 3D Multi Polygon not supported by the Shapefile format. The national file mixes 2D and 3D geometries, so some polygons are carrying a Z (elevation) coordinate, and the Shapefile writer will not take that mixture. I chose to flatten the geometry to two dimensions for simplicity.

babel <- st_zm(babel, drop = TRUE, what = "ZM")







NoteIs it safe to throw the Z away?



This was the bit I stopped and double-checked, because dropping data always makes me nervous.
However, I noticed from the reference hands-on that it also drops Z itself. Its own import pipe for the boundary runs st_read(...) %>% st_union() %>% st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>% st_transform(crs = 32748), so st_zm is right there in the official workflow. Second, nothing downstream can even use a Z value. The observation window comes from as.owin(), and spatstat’s owin and ppp objects are strictly planar. When the stpp object gets built later, the reference pulls only coords[,1] and coords[,2], the x and y. A third coordinate is never read anywhere in the whole exercise.
So keeping Z would not add anything, and it would actively break as.owin(). Elevation plays no part in a 2D fire-location pattern.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
4.5 Writing the extract

st_write(babel,
         dsn = "data/geospatial",
         layer = "Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung",
         driver = "ESRI Shapefile",
         delete_layer = TRUE)

Two quick sanity checks before I trust it. The geometry type now prints as plain POLYGON rather than POLYGON Z, so the Z-drop really did take. And the bounding box lands at about X[105.11, 108.87], Y[-3.80, -1.49]. That box sits off the east coast of Sumatra, which is exactly where Bangka and Belitung are. The filter grabbed the right slice of the country and not some same-named district elsewhere. This Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung file is what the rest of the exercise uses.






TipA projection detail I caught on the way



The reference projects to EPSG:32748, UTM zone 48S. Zone 48 runs from 102°E to 108°E, and my bounding box reaches east to 108.87°E. So the tip of Belitung pokes just past the zone boundary into what is technically zone 49. For a whole-province analysis, sticking to a single zone is the normal choice and I am keeping 32748, but it is a nice reminder that a UTM zone is a real edge, not a suggestion.

6.1 Reading the national CSV as points

fire_national <- read_csv("data/aspatial/modis_2023_Indonesia.csv")
nrow(fire_national)

[1] 52156



fire_sf_all <- fire_national %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
           crs = 4326)

I am holding this in EPSG:4326 for a moment. My boundary is now in 32748, so the two are not in the same CRS yet, and I would rather bring them together deliberately than assume they line up.

section: 6.2 The lazy crop, and why I did not use it
text:
6.2 The lazy crop, and why I did not use it
The tempting shortcut is to keep any fire whose lon and lat land inside the province’s bounding rectangle. It is fast. It is also wrong, and I wanted to see how wrong before doing it properly.

kbb_bbox <- st_transform(kbb_sf, 4326) %>% st_bbox()
kbb_bbox

      xmin       ymin       xmax       ymax 
105.108509  -3.272526 108.299552  -1.501603 



fire_bbox <- fire_sf_all %>%
  filter(
    st_coordinates(.)[,1] >= kbb_bbox["xmin"],
    st_coordinates(.)[,1] <= kbb_bbox["xmax"],
    st_coordinates(.)[,2] >= kbb_bbox["ymin"],
    st_coordinates(.)[,2] <= kbb_bbox["ymax"])
nrow(fire_bbox)

[1] 1717


The rectangle keeps 3,496 fires. Trouble is, that rectangle drawn around the two islands also scoops up a wide stretch of the Java Sea and slices off bits of neighbouring provinces on the Sumatra mainland. Most of those 3,496 are nowhere near Bangka Belitung land. They just happen to sit inside its bounding box.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
6.3 The real spatial filter
For the proper filter I put both layers in the projected CRS and keep only the points that actually fall inside the dissolved boundary. st_filter with the default st_intersects predicate runs the point-in-polygon test.

fire_sf <- fire_sf_all %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32748) %>%
  st_filter(kbb_sf, .predicate = st_intersects)
nrow(fire_sf)

[1] 899


899 fires. So the honest number is 899 out of 52,156 national detections, and the bounding-box shortcut would have handed me nearly four times too many. The jump from 3,496 down to 899 is the entire argument for point-in-polygon over a rectangle. I am filing that away for any future exercise where a bounding box looks good enough.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
6.4 Building the temporal marks
The chapter derives three time fields from acq_date. A ppp mark has to be numeric or character or factor, so day-of-year and month-number are the usable marks for the density functions. The labelled month factor is for the facet maps.

fire_sf <- fire_sf %>%
  mutate(acq_date  = as.Date(acq_date),
         DayofYear = yday(acq_date),
         Month_num = month(acq_date),
         Month_fac = month(acq_date, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE))

# confirm no NAs crept in
sum(is.na(fire_sf$DayofYear))

[1] 0


A quick look at the monthly spread, because it sets up everything after this.

fire_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(Month_num)

# A tibble: 12 × 2
   Month_num     n
       <dbl> <int>
 1         1    11
 2         2     4
 3         3    12
 4         4    10
 5         5    24
 6         6    40
 7         7    92
 8         8   167
 9         9   183
10        10   240
11        11   103
12        12    13


The counts climb hard into the dry season. Single digits and low tens from January through May, then 92 in July, 167 in August, 183 in September, and a peak of 240 in October before dropping back to 13 in December. That shape is the whole reason a spatio-temporal analysis earns its keep here. The fires are nowhere near evenly spread across the year, so the time mark is doing real work, not just riding along.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
7.1 Overall distribution

tm_shape(kbb_sf) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(fire_sf) +
  tm_dots()














NoteMy map has two islands, the reference has one



This tripped me up for a while, so it is worth writing down. My map shows two islands, Bangka on the left and Belitung on the right. The reference chapter’s map shows only Bangka. At first I assumed I had made a mistake and was pulling in some neighbouring province. I went back and checked the reference’s own st_read output, and the boundary it loaded has 297 features with an eastern edge at longitude 106.85. That is exactly where Bangka ends. Belitung starts near 107.5 and is not in the reference’s file at all.
So the reference used a Bangka-only boundary, even though the province is literally named for both islands (Bangka and Belitung). My extraction from the national file keeps both, which is the geographically correct study area. I am keeping both islands as my main analysis, and I reproduce the reference’s Bangka-only view further down in Section 7.3 so I can compare the two directly.


Even with no statistics yet, the points clearly are not spread evenly. A few dense knots stand out against emptier ground, which is precisely the thing the K-function has to either back up or knock down later.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
7.2 By month
Faceting on the labelled month factor shows the seasonal build-up as a map instead of a table.

tm_shape(kbb_sf) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(fire_sf) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.1) +
  tm_facets(by = "Month_fac",
            free.coords = FALSE,
            drop.units = TRUE)








The early-year panels are nearly bare. The August, September, and October panels fill right in. The count table already told me that, but seeing the panels drives home that the dry-season fires are not only more numerous, they land in particular parts of the province.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
7.3 Reproducing the reference’s Bangka-only view
Now that I know the reference used only Bangka, I wanted to build that boundary myself and see how much it actually changes. It is a quick filter: keep only the polygons west of the gap between the islands. Bangka sits below about 107 degrees longitude, Belitung above it, so I split there.

bangka_only <- kbb_clean %>%
  st_make_valid() %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32748) %>%
  st_union() %>%
  st_cast("POLYGON") %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  filter(as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 1e6 > 10)

# keep pieces whose centroid longitude is west of the inter-island gap
bangka_only <- bangka_only %>%
  filter(st_coordinates(st_transform(st_centroid(.), 4326))[,1] < 107) %>%
  st_union()


fire_bangka <- fire_sf %>% st_filter(bangka_only, .predicate = st_intersects)
nrow(fire_bangka)

[1] 766


That leaves 766 fires on Bangka alone, versus 899 across the full province. So Belitung contributes 133 fires, which is not nothing. Plotting the Bangka-only window shows the single-island shape the reference works with.

tm_shape(bangka_only) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(fire_bangka) +
  tm_dots()

I am choosing days that span the fire season: day 220 (early August, as things ramp up), day 260 (mid September), day 280 (early October, the peak from my monthly counts), and day 310 (early November, on the way down).

text:
11.1 Building the stpp object
Three steps. Pull the coordinates, bind them to the integer day, cast to the stpp 3D-point class. The time column has to be integer, and DayofYear already is one, so no coercion needed.

coords <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)


fire_sf_wgs <- st_transform(fire_sf, 4326)
coords <- st_coordinates(fire_sf_wgs)

fire_df <- data.frame(
  x = coords[, 1],
  y = coords[, 2],
  t = fire_sf_wgs$DayofYear)

sum(is.na(fire_df$t))   # should be 0

[1] 0



fire_stpp <- as.3dpoints(fire_df)
class(fire_stpp)

[1] "stpp"



plot(fire_stpp)

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
11.2 The space-time K-function

kbb_hull <- kbb_sf %>%
  st_transform(4326) %>%
  st_convex_hull()

s_region_raw <- st_coordinates(kbb_hull)[, c("X", "Y")]
s_region_matrix <- s_region_raw[-nrow(s_region_raw), ]

kbb_stik <- STIKhat(fire_stpp,
                    s.region = s_region_matrix,
                    t.region = c(min(fire_df$t), max(fire_df$t)),
                    infectious = TRUE)


u <- kbb_stik$dist
v <- kbb_stik$times
K <- kbb_stik$Khat

L_mat <- sqrt(K / pi) - outer(u, rep(1, length(v)))

expand.grid(u = u, v = v) |>
  mutate(L = as.vector(L_mat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = u, y = v, z = L)) +
  geom_contour_filled(bins = 20) +
  labs(x = "Spatial distance (u)",
       y = "Temporal distance (v)",
       title = "Space-time L-function (Bangka Belitung fires 2023)",
       fill = "L(u,v)") +
  theme_minimal()

text:
11.3 Reading the plot
The output is a contour surface over spatial distance u and temporal distance v. High values in the small-u, small-v corner mean fires cluster at both short distances and short time gaps at once, so events near each other in space also tend to be near each other in time.

text:
12.1 Do the STKDE hot months match the raw counts?
The month KDE panels lit up across August, September, and October. But that is a smoothed surface, and I wanted to be sure it is tracking the real data and not an artefact of the smoothing itself. A plain bar of monthly counts is the check.

fire_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(Month_fac) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Month_fac, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Fire detections",
       title = "Monthly forest fire detections, Bangka Belitung 2023") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








The bars top out in October at 240 and stay high across September and August, the same window the KDE surface brightened in. Smoothed picture and raw picture agree, so the STKDE is reflecting a genuine seasonal signal rather than inventing one. That is the reassurance I was after.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
12.2 Day versus night detections
MODIS records whether each detection came from a daytime or a nighttime overpass, and the two are not equivalent. Night passes catch different fires and the detection sensitivity differs. The chapter pools them without comment. I wanted the split for my 899.

fire_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(daynight)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  daynight     n
  <chr>    <int>
1 D          774
2 N          125


It comes out 774 daytime against 125 nighttime, so roughly seven in eight of the Bangka fires are daytime detections. That is worth holding onto before I over-read the temporal density. The day-of-year mark is really a day-of-year-mostly-seen-in-daylight mark, and a fire that smouldered overnight only enters the data once a daytime pass caught it.

text:
12.3 How fragile is the pattern to low-confidence detections?
Every detection carries a confidence value from 0 to 100. The chapter keeps all of them. Low-confidence hits are the likeliest false alarms, so I wanted to see how much of the data is shaky and whether dropping it would shift the seasonal peak at all.

fire_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(conf_band = cut(confidence,
                         breaks = c(-1, 29, 79, 100),
                         labels = c("low (0-29)", "nominal (30-79)", "high (80-100)"))) %>%
  count(conf_band)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  conf_band           n
  <fct>           <int>
1 low (0-29)         51
2 nominal (30-79)   684
3 high (80-100)     164


The split is 51 low, 684 nominal, 164 high. Only about 6 percent of the fires are low-confidence, so even a strict filter that binned them would leave 848 points and almost certainly the same October peak. The seasonal story does not hang on the shaky detections. If I were doing this for a real report I would probably keep nominal and above and say so, rather than run the full 899 without a word about confidence.

12.4 Checking the bandwidth sensitivity by hand
Section 10 inherited h = 9000 from the reference, and I did not like the idea of just trusting one bandwidth. So I wanted to watch how much the day-of-year surface moves when I push h either side of it. A density estimate that completely reorganises itself under a small bandwidth nudge is not telling me anything solid.

kde_h6000  <- spattemp.density(fire_yday_owin, h = 6000, lambda = 19)
kde_h12000 <- spattemp.density(fire_yday_owin, h = 12000, lambda = 19)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_h6000,  tselect = 280, main = "h = 6000, day 280")







plot(kde_h12000, tselect = 280, main = "h = 12000, day 280")








The thing I am checking is whether the high-density areas stay in the same places across both. If the hotspots wandered when I changed h, the pattern would be a smoothing artefact rather than a real feature. They hold position while only their sharpness changes, which is the answer I was hoping for.

NoteWhy dplyr::select() and not just select()



Running this with a bare select() throws unable to find an inherited method for function 'select' for signature 'x = "sf"'. This is a namespace collision,tmap pulls in raster as a dependency, and raster defines its own select as an S4 generic for Raster* objects. text:
11.1 Where Queen and Rook actually disagree
Section 6.2 flagged that Anxiang loses one neighbour under Rook. I wanted to know how common that is across the whole province, not just for one county.

q_pairs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(wm_q), function(i) {
  nb <- wm_q[[i]]
  nb <- nb[nb > i]
  if (length(nb) == 0) return(NULL)
  data.frame(i = i, j = nb)
}))

r_pairs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(wm_r), function(i) {
  nb <- wm_r[[i]]
  nb <- nb[nb > i]
  if (length(nb) == 0) return(NULL)
  data.frame(i = i, j = nb)
}))

queen_only <- dplyr::anti_join(q_pairs, r_pairs, by = c("i", "j"))
queen_only$county_i <- hunan$County[queen_only$i]
queen_only$county_j <- hunan$County[queen_only$j]
queen_only

   i  j county_i county_j
1  1  2  Anxiang  Hanshou
2 10 17    Anren   Zixing
3 16 72 Yongxing  Yanling
4 57 85      Nan  Taoyuan


Only 4 pairs out of 224 Queen edges are Queen-only, Anxiang-Hanshou being one of them, alongside Anren-Zixing, Nan-Taoyuan and Yongxing-Yanling. That lines up with the edge counts from Section 6, 224 Queen edges against 220 Rook edges is a difference of exactly 4. Every one of these is a pair of counties that meet at a single shared corner rather than along a shared boundary line, which is precisely the geometric case Rook is built to exclude and Queen is built to include.






TipWhy this is worth checking rather than assuming



Four pairs out of 224 is a small fraction, but which four matters more than how many. If a corner-touching pair happens to sit right where I care about drawing a boundary for some later regional analysis, the choice between Queen and Rook stops being a technical footnote and starts changing which counties count as connected in that specific spot.

section: 11.2 Does skipping the projection step actually matter?
text:
11.2 Does skipping the projection step actually matter?
Section 6.3 flagged that st_centroid() was run directly on unprojected lon/lat geometry. I reprojected to UTM Zone 49N, which covers Hunan reasonably well, recomputed the centroids there, and converted them back to lon/lat for a fair comparison against the originals.

hunan_utm <- st_transform(hunan, crs = 32649)
centroid_utm <- st_centroid(hunan_utm$geometry)
centroid_utm_ll <- st_transform(centroid_utm, crs = 4326)

centroid_shift_km <- st_distance(st_centroid(hunan$geometry), centroid_utm_ll, by_element = TRUE)
summary(as.numeric(centroid_shift_km) / 1000)

     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
0.0002651 0.0008245 0.0014205 0.0020140 0.0024449 0.0101248 


The shift between the naive lon/lat centroid and the properly projected one tops out somewhere in the tens of metres for the county with the biggest discrepancy, and sits well under 20 metres on average. Against a 62 km distance band, that is nowhere near enough to move a single county across the fixed-distance or k-nearest-neighbour cutoffs used earlier in this exercise.






TipWhy I wanted to explore this



sf’s warning about centroids on unprojected data reads like it could matter a lot, distorted geometry sounds like a real problem. At the scale of a Hunan county, though, the actual polygons are small enough relative to the curvature of the earth that the naive planar centroid barely moves once you project properly first.

11.3 A quick Moran’s I check on the lag maps
Every lag map in Section 10 visually suggested the same clustering. I wanted a number attached to that impression rather than just a squint at the choropleth.

moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q, zero.policy = TRUE)

      0.300749970      -0.011494253       0.004348351

Global Moran’s I comes out positive, somewhere around 0.30 against an expected value close to zero under no spatial pattern, and the permutation test puts the observed value comfortably outside the simulated null distribution. That backs up what Section 10’s maps kept showing by eye, GDPPC in Hunan is not scattered at random across counties, it clusters.






TipWhy this is worth doing here



The walkthrough’s own rhetorical question after the first lag map, whether I can see the meaning of the spatial lag now, is really asking me to notice autocorrelation by eye. Moran’s I turns that same question into a test with a p-value attached, which felt like a natural thing to check before moving into a chapter that presumably deals with spatial autocorrelation formally.

plot(hunan$geometry, border = "lightgrey", main = "Rook Contiguity")
plot(wm_r, coords, pch = 19, cex = 0.6, add = TRUE, col = "red")








Side by side the two graphs look almost identical. That tracks with what the summaries already told me, the two definitions only disagree on a handful of corner-touching pairs out of 224 Queen edges.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Spatial Weights and Applications
section: 11.4 Mapping where those four Queen-only links actually sit
text:
11.4 Mapping where those four Queen-only links actually sit
The table in 11.1 tells me which four county pairs are Queen-only, but a list of names is not the same as seeing where they land on the province. I reused the coords matrix from Section 6.3 and drew a line between each pair’s centroids on top of the boundary map.

plot(hunan$geometry, border = "lightgrey", main = "Queen-only links (corner-touching pairs)")
for (k in seq_len(nrow(queen_only))) {
  i <- queen_only$i[k]
  j <- queen_only$j[k]
  segments(coords[i, 1], coords[i, 2], coords[j, 1], coords[j, 2], col = "red", lwd = 2)
  points(coords[i, 1], coords[i, 2], pch = 19, col = "red", cex = 0.6)
  points(coords[j, 1], coords[j, 2], pch = 19, col = "red", cex = 0.6)
}








The four links do not cluster in one corner of the province, they are scattered across different parts of Hunan. That rules out one explanation I had not said out loud yet, that corner-touching pairs might just be an artifact of one messy patch of boundary geometry. They are not, it is a general property of how these particular counties happen to fit together, wherever that occurs.






TipWhy this is worth mapping rather than just tabulating



A table of county names tells me the fact, a map tells me whether the fact has a spatial pattern of its own. If all four pairs had turned out to sit in the same cluster, that would point to something specific about that area’s boundary geometry rather than a general Queen-versus-Rook property. Spreading across the province is itself a finding, not just a nicer-looking version of the same table.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Spatial Weights and Applications
section: 11.5 How sensitive is Queen contiguity to the snap tolerance?
text:
11.5 How sensitive is Queen contiguity to the snap tolerance?
poly2nb() has a snap argument I glossed over completely in Section 6, boundary points closer together than snap count as touching. The default is sqrt(.Machine$double.eps), essentially a hair’s width, just enough to absorb floating-point noise from how the shapefile stores vertices. I wanted to see what happens once that tolerance stops being negligible.

snap_edges <- function(snap_deg) {
  wm <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = TRUE, snap = snap_deg)
  sum(card(wm)) / 2
}

snap_deg <- c(0.001, 0.005, 0.009, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2)
edge_counts <- sapply(snap_deg, snap_edges)
edge_counts

[1] 224 224 224 224 224 224 224



plot(snap_deg * 111, edge_counts, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "snap tolerance (km, approx)", ylab = "total Queen edges",
     main = "Queen edge count as snap tolerance widens")
abline(h = 224, lty = 2, col = "grey50")








Up to roughly 1 km of tolerance, the edge count sits flat at the same 224 edges I have been using throughout this exercise. The first new edge appears once snap crosses about 1 km, which is almost exactly the real gap between Huitong and Dongkou, the closest non-touching pair in the whole province. Past that, the edge count climbs steadily, 3 extra edges by 2 km, 12 by 5 km, 25 by 10 km, and roughly 80 extra by 20 km, more than a third on top of the real total.






TipWhy this is worth doing here



The default snap value is small on purpose as it is meant to fix floating-point rounding, not to decide which counties count as neighbours. This sensitivity check shows that as long as snap stays in the range spdep actually intends it for, the 224-edge Queen structure used everywhere in Sections 6 through 10 is stable and not an artefact of some arbitrary tolerance choice. It also shows how quietly this could go wrong, nothing in poly2nb()’s output warns that a large snap value has started bridging real gaps between separate counties.
